title: ABA Take Down in the News Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://specialeducationtoday.substack.com
author: Special Education Today
summary: Special Education Today responds to a NY Times investigation alleging that Applied Behavior Analysis therapy clinics overprescribe treatment to young children with autism, some spending up to 40 hours per week in facilities. The article's primary contribution is a letter to the NY Times authors defending ABA as one of the most evidence-based interventions for students with disabilities, particularly those with severe autism, when implemented correctly. The letter argues that the NY Times conflated ineffective or poor implementation with the therapy itself — that when ABA is not working, the cause is almost always implementation quality rather than the methodology's effectiveness. ABA is defended as teaching communication, social, and academic skills most effectively in real-life settings (home and school) with family members and peers, not as an isolated clinic-based intervention. The letter specifically directs readers to the UNC AFIRM website's free training in evidence-based ABA interventions and to Steinbrenner et al. (2020) for a systematic review of evidence-based practices. The broader concern from the newsletter is that fraudulent billing and poor implementation by some ABA providers have generated a media narrative that may reduce access to a genuinely effective therapeutic approach for families who need it.
points: The NY Times framing — 'effectiveness is mixed' — is challenged on the grounds that it confuses the outcome of poor implementation with the outcome of the methodology itself; well-implemented, individualized ABA with continuous data collection has a robust evidence base.

ABA is most effective when it is embedded in real-life contexts (home, school, community) with consistent involvement of caregivers and teachers, not as a clinical intervention isolated from the child's natural environment.

The breadth of evidence-based ABA practices is often not understood by critics: the approach encompasses communication interventions, exercise-based approaches, cognitive-behavioral techniques, and social skills training, not merely the drill-and-reward procedures critics associate with it.

The fraudulent billing problem — providers charging for services not delivered — is a real and serious issue that the newsletter has tracked since 2021, but it is distinct from the question of whether well-implemented ABA is effective, and the two must not be conflated.

Free, accessible resources for evidence-based ABA implementation exist (UNC AFIRM website, Peabody Vanderbilt videos) — the barrier is not evidence but knowledge dissemination to practitioners and families.
quotes: I very much appreciate your highlighting this therapy for children with Autism, but I strongly disagree with the statement that the effectiveness of ABA therapy is mixed.

Indeed, ABA therapy is one of the most effective strategies for teaching students with disabilities, including those who experience severe Autism. Through ABA therapy, students learn communication, social, and academic skills.
The therapy is most effective when conducted in real-life settings, such as home and school, with family members and peers.

If the therapy is not working, as your article suggests, then that is likely due to ineffective or poor implementation. ABA requires work and consistency on the part of the therapist, the caregiver, and the child.

Interventions must be tailored to meet the needs of the child and family — this tailoring is informed by continuous data collection. When implemented correctly, ABA therapy has made a significant difference in the lives of people with disabilities.
Note the breadth of these interventions — from communication to exercise to cognitive-behavioral approaches — these interventions are all grounded in ABA.
